title: The sand mandala
hook: monks build a mandala of colored sand for days, then sweep it into a river

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara, and your line, she comes quickly. When someone asked for help, did you answer a little faster? Day three hundred fourteen.

A museum lobby, or a college gym. A small group of Tibetan monks has set up a low table. For days, sometimes weeks, they lean over it, tapping thin metal funnels, and grains of colored sand trickle out a few at a time. People come back every afternoon to watch it grow: palaces, gates, lotus petals, sharp lines finer than a pencil could draw. Then, on the last day, with everyone watching, a monk draws a line straight through the middle. Today: the sand mandala.
screen: `A LOW TABLE, A FEW MONKS.` → `SAND, A FEW GRAINS AT A TIME.` → `A LINE THROUGH THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Mandala is Sanskrit for circle. In Tibetan practice it's more than a pattern: it's a map of an awakened world, often the palace of a Buddha or deity seen from above, with four gates facing the four directions, walls in bright colors, and the deity at the very center. People meditate on it, and some rituals are performed around it. Mandalas can be painted, or built in three dimensions, or pictured in the mind. The sand mandala is made to be fragile. Monks use a narrow metal funnel with ridges along its side; rubbing a rod across the ridges makes it vibrate, and the sand falls grain by grain. Teams work from the center outward, following exact measurements handed down in the texts. It can take days, or weeks. And then the ending, which is the part people remember. When the rituals are complete, the lines are cut through and the sand is swept toward the center into one gray-brown pile. Some is given to the people watching, as a blessing. The rest is carried to a river or stream and poured into the water, so the blessing flows out into the world, like the wind through the prayer flags. Why build something so beautiful and then destroy it? Tibetan teachers give more than one reason. The sweeping teaches impermanence, which you've met since the first sight of an old man. It teaches letting go of what we make. And it shows that the blessing was never meant to stay in one room. The work was real. The beauty was real. And it's swept away.
screen: `MANDALA — CIRCLE, A MAP OF AWAKENING.` · `SAND, GRAIN BY GRAIN, FOR DAYS.` · `SWEPT TO THE CENTER.` · `POURED INTO THE RIVER.` · then, large: `SWEPT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, make something small. Arrange a few objects on a table into a pattern: coins, pens, leaves, whatever's near. Take care with it, just for a moment. Look at it. Then gently mix it up, and let it go. Notice any small tug of not wanting to. Then sit, and let each breath arrive and pass, built and swept away. The bell holds the time.
Mandala. A circle: a map of an awakened world, built in sand with great care, then swept away and poured into the river.
Your line: swept away. Today, do one thing well that won't last, a meal, a clean counter, a kind message, and let it go without needing it to stay. Day three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Tibetan monks construct sand mandalas for particular rituals and, increasingly, for public events; when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala, give some sand to those present and pour the rest into flowing water.

original.note: Sanskrit maṇḍala: circle. Tibetan: kyilkhor, 'center and surround'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty circular pattern.
what it means: a map of an awakened world, built with care and then swept away.
what a scholar hears: the Tibetan dul tsön kyilkhor, 'mandala of colored powder', follows measurements in tantric texts such as the Kalachakra, and its dissolution is itself part of the ritual.

sources.ref: Tibetan ritual practice of the sand mandala (e.g. the Kalachakra mandala)
